content:
Exercise is a core treatment for knee osteoarthritis, but there is no single home programme that is best for everyone. Your starting point depends on your symptoms, strength, balance, other conditions and what you want to be able to do. A manageable plan that you can repeat is more useful than trying to complete a demanding list on the first day.

This guide is for adults with knee osteoarthritis. It is not a rehabilitation plan after a knee replacement or a recent injury. Follow your surgical or physiotherapy team's advice if you have been given a specific programme.

What does NICE recommend for knee osteoarthritis?

NICE NG226, recommendations 1.3.1 to 1.3.4, recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to each person's needs. This includes strengthening muscles around the affected joint and general aerobic fitness. Supervised sessions can help, and exercise may be combined with education or support to build a routine.

NICE also explains that joint pain may increase when you start. Regular, consistent exercise can reduce pain and improve function and quality of life over time. That does not mean you should push through severe pain, a new injury or a suddenly hot, swollen joint.

There is no strength-percentage target or guaranteed recovery week in this guidance. A stronger thigh does not guarantee a particular amount of pain relief. Look at changes in daily activities as well as strength: getting out of a chair, walking to a shop or managing the stairs may matter most to you.

How should you prepare for home exercises?

Choose a clear space and a stable chair that will not slide or tip. Wear comfortable clothes and supportive footwear for standing exercises. Keep a firm support within reach. If getting down to the floor or back up is difficult, use a suitable bed for lying exercises or ask a physiotherapist for seated alternatives.

A short, gentle walk can help you warm up if walking is comfortable. Do not make standing exercises a balance test. If your knee gives way, you have had falls or you do not feel steady even with support, ask for an assessment before trying standing exercises on your own.

Which knee exercises can you try at home?

The examples below are drawn from NHS knee and strength-exercise guidance. They are options, not a requirement to do every exercise. Start with movements that you can control comfortably. A physiotherapist can check your technique and help you choose the right exercises and amount.

Seated knee straightening

Sit upright on a stable chair with your feet on the floor. Slowly straighten one knee, keeping the movement controlled. Bring the foot back down gently. Work within your comfortable range rather than forcing the knee straight. Repeat on the other side if appropriate.

Heel slide

Lie comfortably on your back. Slide one heel towards your bottom so the knee bends, then slide it away again. Use a small range at first if the knee is stiff. Do not force the bend or pull through sharp pain.

Knee straightening over a rolled towel

Lie on your back with a small rolled towel under one knee. Tighten the front of your thigh and lift your foot by straightening the knee while keeping the knee supported on the towel. Lower the foot slowly and relax. This works the thigh muscles; it is not a way to isolate or repair one specific part of the joint.

Supported calf raise

Stand with both hands on a stable support. Slowly lift your heels, keeping your weight controlled, then lower them. Use both legs and keep the support. If you cannot stay steady or the movement increases knee pain, stop and ask about an alternative.

Supported shallow squat

Hold a stable support with your feet about hip-width apart. Bend your knees a little, keeping them pointing forwards, then slowly return to standing. Use a comfortable depth. You do not need to reach a particular angle or progress to a deep squat for this to count as exercise.

How many repetitions and sessions should you do?

The amount needs to fit you. NHS leaflets give different starting amounts and frequencies because they cover different exercises and people. NICE does not prescribe one daily set-and-repetition schedule for everyone.

For example, Dynamic Health's knee osteoarthritis guidance suggests starting with one set of 3 to 4 repetitions and building towards 8 to 10 as strength improves. The national NHS general strength page uses 5 repetitions for several standing exercises and suggests strength exercise at least twice a week. These are starting examples, not targets you must meet despite symptoms.

You may need fewer repetitions or a smaller movement to begin with. Build up slowly, allow recovery between harder sessions and change one part of the exercise at a time. If an exercise has become easy, discuss whether to increase repetitions, range or resistance. Do not add ankle weights simply because a fixed number of weeks has passed.

What if exercise makes your knee hurt?

Some discomfort can happen when starting exercise. Notice how your knee feels during the session, afterwards, that night and the following day. If the exercise causes sharp pain, much more pain than usual, increased swelling, disturbed sleep or difficulty with normal activities, reduce the amount or stop that exercise and seek advice if symptoms do not settle.

There is no universal pain score or two-hour rule that makes every exercise safe for every person. Local NHS programmes use different symptom-monitoring rules. Follow the plan agreed with your physiotherapist and do not use a pain number to ignore a clear change in your symptoms.

During a familiar osteoarthritis flare, you may need to reduce the load or choose gentler movement. A new, suddenly hot or swollen knee is different and needs assessment rather than simply a rest day. Do not continue a programme unchanged while waiting for unexplained severe symptoms to pass.

Should you also walk, cycle or swim?

Strengthening is only part of the plan. NICE includes general aerobic fitness, and NHS advice includes walking, cycling and swimming as possible activities. Choose something you enjoy and can manage. Shorter sessions spread through the day may be easier than one long session.

If walking aggravates your knee, ask about a different activity, pacing or a walking aid. A physiotherapist can help you find an approach that fits your balance, other joints and general health. Do not replace an individual postoperative plan with this general guide.

When should you ask for physiotherapy or a review?

Ask for help if you cannot find a tolerable starting point, keep flaring after exercise, have balance problems or are not sure how to progress. In many areas, NHS community musculoskeletal services accept self-referrals. Check the route in your area or ask your GP practice.

There is no guaranteed week when stiffness or pain will improve. Track a few things that matter to you, such as chair rises, walking distance, sleep and swelling. Take the notes to your review so the plan can be adjusted. Persistent or worsening pain deserves a review, not a judgement that you have failed at exercise.

When does knee pain need urgent help?

Get urgent advice from NHS 111 if your knee is very painful, you cannot move it or put weight on it, it is badly swollen or has changed shape, or it locks, gives way or painfully clicks. Sudden severe pain with a hot or swollen joint needs urgent GP or NHS 111 assessment. Joint infection can occur without a fever.

Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, collapse or chest pain that could be a heart attack. Do not exercise through these symptoms. This guide is educational information, not a diagnosis or a personal treatment plan.

Related guidance

See our knee exercise guide, beginner strength guide and guide to physiotherapy while waiting. Confirm an exercise plan with your healthcare team when you need personal advice.

key_takeaways: NICE recommends exercise tailored to your needs, including strengthening and aerobic activity.
Choose manageable exercises and build up gradually rather than following a fixed progression calendar.
A new hot, swollen or severely painful knee needs assessment, even without a fever.
Ask a physiotherapist for help with technique, balance, symptoms or progression.

faq.q: What exercises does NICE recommend for knee osteoarthritis?
faq.a: NICE recommends exercise tailored to your needs, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. Supervised sessions may help. There is no single best programme for everyone.

faq.q: How many knee exercise repetitions should I do at home?
faq.a: Start with an amount you can manage and build up slowly. NHS programmes use different examples. Follow an individual plan if you have one, and ask a physiotherapist if you cannot find a tolerable starting point.

faq.q: Should I keep exercising if my knee hurts?
faq.a: Some initial discomfort can occur, but do not push through sharp pain, much worse symptoms or increased swelling. Reduce or stop the aggravating exercise and get advice if symptoms do not settle. A new hot or swollen joint needs urgent assessment.

faq.q: How quickly will knee osteoarthritis exercises help?
faq.a: There is no guaranteed week for improvement. Regular exercise can improve pain and function over time. Track daily activities and ask for a review if symptoms persist or worsen.
